facts.text: Whitesboro was settled in the late 1800s by Steve White, becoming one of Etowah County’s earliest communities after the county formed in 1866.
Etowah County, where Whitesboro sits, was renamed in 1868 from Baine County to a Cherokee word meaning "edible tree," reflecting Native American roots.
Unlike neighboring Gadsden, Whitesboro has stayed agricultural, with residents mainly farming the county’s hilly terrain.
The area’s early settlers followed treaties like the 1816 Turkeytown agreement, opening Cherokee lands for farming of edible crops.
Whitesboro sits at about 1,063 feet above sea level, nestled among Sand Mountain and Lookout Mountain foothills.
During World War II, nearby Gadsden’s ordnance plant and Camp Sibert drew workers from Whitesboro, briefly diversifying its economy.
